## Question 118 — Cache lifetimes

**Module:** Module 6 – RTK Query  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 5–8 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
Explain **Cache lifetimes**, including why it exists, where it belongs in a React application, its runtime/data-flow implications, and the trade-offs an enterprise team should consider.

### Definition
The key production concern is server-state ownership: cache identity, freshness, invalidation, cancellation, retries and synchronization should be handled by a query/cache abstraction rather than copied into unrelated global UI state.

### Overview
State management is primarily an ownership and synchronization problem. A good design identifies the authoritative source, the consumers, the update path, the failure model and the lifecycle of the data.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents duplicated or conflicting state.
- Makes rendering behavior predictable.
- Enables testable business logic and observable production behavior.
- Supports scaling from a single feature to large multi-team applications.

### Architecture
```text
Feature
 ├── UI components
 ├── State / cache boundary
 ├── Selectors / query hooks
 ├── Domain logic
 └── API / repository
          ↓
     Backend services
```

### Internal Workflow
An update enters through a UI event or external synchronization source, passes through the selected state/cache boundary, updates immutable or reactive state, notifies relevant subscribers, and causes React to render the affected consumers.

### Data Flow
```text
Intent
  ↓
Action / Mutation
  ↓
Middleware / Network
  ↓
Reducer OR Query Cache
  ↓
Subscription / Selector
  ↓
React Render
```

### Performance Characteristics
- Prefer narrow subscriptions and selectors.
- Avoid duplicating server state in multiple stores.
- Measure render fan-out and cache growth.
- Batch related updates when the library/runtime supports it.
- Remove stale listeners and unused cache entries.

### Memory Considerations
- Large normalized stores can retain unused entities.
- Query caches require explicit freshness and garbage-collection policies.
- Subscriptions must be cleaned up.
- Persisted state should be intentionally scoped and versioned.

### React Integration
Use typed hooks or query hooks at feature boundaries. Keep presentational components focused on rendering and user interaction; keep domain/state logic in reusable feature modules.

### Production Use Case
A production team can use **Cache lifetimes** to make ownership explicit, reduce unnecessary renders, isolate failure boundaries and establish consistent debugging and testing workflows.

### Enterprise Example
In a multi-team application, the shared state contract should be versioned and documented. Domain state, server cache, authentication, UI state and analytics should not become one undifferentiated global store.

### Code Example 1
```tsx
import { createApi, fetchBaseQuery } from "@reduxjs/toolkit/query/react";

type User = { id: string; name: string };

export const usersApi = createApi({
  reducerPath: "usersApi",
  baseQuery: fetchBaseQuery({ baseUrl: "/api" }),
  tagTypes: ["User"],
  endpoints: (build) => ({
    getUser: build.query<User, string>({
      query: (id) => `/users/${id}`,
      providesTags: (_result, _error, id) => [{ type: "User", id }],
    }),
  }),
});

export const { useGetUserQuery } = usersApi;
```

### Code Example 2
```tsx
// Keep server data in a query cache rather than duplicating it in global UI state.
const queryKey = ["users", { page: 1, filter: "active" }] as const;
// Stable query keys make cache identity explicit.
console.log(queryKey);
// ["users", { page: 1, filter: "active" }]
```

### Advanced Production Example
```tsx
// Feature-based boundary: keep state access behind a small public API.
export type Order = {
  id: string;
  status: "pending" | "paid" | "failed";
};

export function selectOrderStatus(
  orders: Record<string, Order>,
  id: string,
): Order["status"] | "unknown" {
  return orders[id]?.status ?? "unknown";
}
```

### Folder Structure
```text
src/
├── app/
│   ├── store.ts
│   └── providers/
├── features/
│   └── orders/
│       ├── components/
│       ├── hooks/
│       ├── api/
│       ├── selectors/
│       ├── model/
│       └── tests/
├── shared/
│   ├── ui/
│   └── types/
└── infrastructure/
    ├── logging/
    └── analytics/
```

### Expected Output
The state transition is deterministic and only the consumers that depend on the changed state should need to update. Server data should remain synchronized through the selected cache/query abstraction.

### ASCII State Diagram
```text
             ┌───────────────┐
             │   React UI    │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Intent/Event  │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │ Store / Query Cache     │
        └───────────┬─────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Selectors /   │
             │ Query Hooks   │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
                 React UI
```

### Performance Notes
Use React DevTools Profiler to identify expensive renders and library-specific DevTools to inspect state/cache transitions. Optimize subscription granularity before introducing complex memoization.

### Security Considerations
- Never treat UI state as an authorization boundary.
- Do not persist secrets unnecessarily.
- Redact tokens and personal data from logs and DevTools captures.
- Validate server responses before storing them in sensitive workflows.

### Advantages
- Explicit state ownership
- Predictable updates
- Strong debugging options
- Testable architecture
- Scales when boundaries are well designed

### Disadvantages
- Additional abstraction and learning cost
- Poorly designed global state can become tightly coupled
- Cache invalidation and synchronization are complex

### Trade-offs
| Requirement | Prefer | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Local UI | React state | Global store |
| Server data | RTK Query / TanStack Query / Apollo | Manual duplicate cache |
| Cross-cutting low-frequency config | Context | Giant global store |
| Complex client workflows | Redux Toolkit / state machine | Scattered effects |
| Tiny isolated store | Zustand / Jotai | Heavy architecture without need |

### Best Practices
1. Define ownership before selecting a library.
2. Keep server state in a server-state cache.
3. Normalize large relational client state when appropriate.
4. Keep selectors focused.
5. Prefer feature boundaries.
6. Instrument important transitions.
7. Test behavior, not implementation details.

### Anti-patterns
- One global store for everything
- Duplicating query data into Redux without a clear reason
- Persisting sensitive tokens by default
- Storing derived values that can be computed
- Calling network APIs directly from arbitrary UI components

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing client state with server state.
- Overusing Context for high-frequency updates.
- Mutating state outside the library's supported mechanisms.
- Ignoring cache invalidation.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce the state transition.
2. Inspect the action/event or query mutation.
3. Inspect the store/cache before and after.
4. Check selector outputs.
5. Profile affected React components.
6. Inspect network requests and cache headers.
7. Check for duplicated subscriptions or stale closures.

### Common Interview Traps
- 'Redux is only for global state.'
- 'Context replaces Redux in every application.'
- 'React Query is a global state manager.'
- 'More memoization always improves performance.'
- 'Frontend role checks are authorization.'

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
Your enterprise React application is experiencing inconsistent data and unnecessary renders related to **Cache lifetimes**. How would you redesign ownership, synchronization, caching and component subscriptions?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the authoritative source of truth?
2. Is this client state or server state?
3. What happens under concurrent updates?
4. How is stale data invalidated?
5. How would you test failure and recovery?
6. What is the memory/caching cost?
7. How would this scale across 20 frontend teams?

### System Design Discussion
Define state domains, ownership boundaries, API contracts, cache policy, persistence policy, cross-tab behavior, observability, testing strategy, migration strategy and rollback plan.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] State has a clear owner
- [ ] Server state is not unnecessarily duplicated
- [ ] Updates are predictable and immutable
- [ ] Selectors/subscriptions are appropriately narrow
- [ ] Loading/error/empty states exist
- [ ] Sensitive data is protected
- [ ] Tests cover success and failure
- [ ] Production telemetry is available

### 30-second Interview Answer
**Cache lifetimes** should be chosen based on state ownership and lifecycle. I would first classify the state, then select the smallest suitable mechanism, define the update/cache policy, and validate performance and failure behavior with profiling and tests.

### 2-minute Interview Answer
Start with what **Cache lifetimes** solves, then explain the data flow and subscription model. Compare it with the alternatives, discuss cache and memory behavior, and finish with how you would test, monitor, secure and migrate it in production.

### 5-minute Deep Explanation
At Staff/Principal level, discuss **Cache lifetimes** as architecture rather than API syntax: ownership, consistency, synchronization, cache invalidation, update fan-out, memory retention, failure recovery, observability, team boundaries, deployment/migration risk and long-term maintainability.

### Assignments
Design a feature architecture demonstrating **Cache lifetimes**. Document state ownership, cache policy, error states, performance budget, testing strategy and migration/rollback strategy.

### Mini Project
Build an enterprise dashboard with authentication, server data, filters, optimistic updates, caching, error recovery and a feature flag. Keep UI, server and persistent state explicitly separated.

### MCQs
1. Which is usually server state?  
A. Modal open  B. API user profile  C. Selected tab  D. Input draft  
**Answer: B**
2. What is a selector primarily useful for?  
A. CSS  B. Narrowing derived/read state  C. Authentication  D. Routing  
**Answer: B**
3. Which tool is designed primarily for server-state caching?  
A. TanStack Query  B. CSS Modules  C. React Router  D. ESLint  
**Answer: A**
4. What is a key Redux Toolkit benefit?  
A. Removes JavaScript  B. Simplifies predictable Redux architecture  C. Replaces HTTP  D. Eliminates React rendering  
**Answer: B**
5. What should be the security boundary for authorization?  
A. UI store  B. CSS  C. Backend/server  D. Selector  
**Answer: C**

### Coding Exercise
Implement **Cache lifetimes** using TypeScript and React 19+. Include loading, error and empty states, a test, and a performance note.

### Debugging Exercise
Create an intentionally inefficient state flow, profile it, identify the update fan-out, then reduce unnecessary subscriptions and verify the improvement.

### Revision Notes
- Cache lifetimes: definition → ownership → data flow → rendering → performance → security → testing → architecture.
- Always distinguish source of truth from derived state.
- Measure before optimizing.

### Cheat Sheet
**Cache lifetimes → Who owns it? → Who updates it? → Who reads it? → How is it cached? → How is it persisted? → How does it fail?**

```tsx
type State = {
  selectedId: string | null;
};

const initialState: State = { selectedId: null };

export function selectItem(state: State, id: string): State {
  return { ...state, selectedId: id };
}

console.log(selectItem(initialState, "item-1"));
// { selectedId: "item-1" }
```

### Code Example 2
```tsx

const next = {

};

console.log(state.user.name); // Asha
console.log(next.user.name);  // Maya
```

3. Normalize large relational client state when appropriate.
4. Keep selectors focused.
5. Prefer feature boundaries.
6. Instrument important transitions.
7. Test behavior, not implementation details.

### Anti-patterns
- One global store for everything
- Duplicating query data into Redux without a clear reason
- Persisting sensitive tokens by default
- Storing derived values that can be computed
- Calling network APIs directly from arbitrary UI components

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing client state with server state.
- Overusing Context for high-frequency updates.
- Mutating state outside the library's supported mechanisms.
- Ignoring cache invalidation.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce the state transition.
2. Inspect the action/event or query mutation.
3. Inspect the store/cache before and after.
4. Check selector outputs.
5. Profile affected React components.
6. Inspect network requests and cache headers.
7. Check for duplicated subscriptions or stale closures.

### Common Interview Traps
- 'Redux is only for global state.'
- 'Context replaces Redux in every application.'
- 'React Query is a global state manager.'
- 'More memoization always improves performance.'
- 'Frontend role checks are authorization.'

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
Your enterprise React application is experiencing inconsistent data and unnecessary renders related to **RTK Query architecture**. How would you redesign ownership, synchronization, caching and component subscriptions?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the authoritative source of truth?
2. Is this client state or server state?
3. What happens under concurrent updates?
4. How is stale data invalidated?
5. How would you test failure and recovery?
6. What is the memory/caching cost?
7. How would this scale across 20 frontend teams?

### System Design Discussion
Define state domains, ownership boundaries, API contracts, cache policy, persistence policy, cross-tab behavior, observability, testing strategy, migration strategy and rollback plan.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] State has a clear owner
- [ ] Server state is not unnecessarily duplicated
- [ ] Updates are predictable and immutable
- [ ] Selectors/subscriptions are appropriately narrow
- [ ] Loading/error/empty states exist
- [ ] Sensitive data is protected
- [ ] Tests cover success and failure
- [ ] Production telemetry is available

### 30-second Interview Answer
**RTK Query architecture** should be chosen based on state ownership and lifecycle. I would first classify the state, then select the smallest suitable mechanism, define the update/cache policy, and validate performance and failure behavior with profiling and tests.

### 2-minute Interview Answer

# Module 7 – Context API vs Redux

**Questions 121–135**

## Question 121 — Context fundamentals

**Module:** Module 7 – Context API vs Redux  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 5–8 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
Explain **Context fundamentals**, including why it exists, where it belongs in a React application, its runtime/data-flow implications, and the trade-offs an enterprise team should consider.

### Definition
Context is excellent for low-frequency cross-cutting values. Frequent, broad updates can cause many consumers to render, so split providers or use an external store when measured fan-out becomes costly.

### Overview
State management is primarily an ownership and synchronization problem. A good design identifies the authoritative source, the consumers, the update path, the failure model and the lifecycle of the data.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents duplicated or conflicting state.
- Makes rendering behavior predictable.
- Enables testable business logic and observable production behavior.
- Supports scaling from a single feature to large multi-team applications.

### Architecture
```text
Feature
 ├── UI components
 ├── State / cache boundary
 ├── Selectors / query hooks
 ├── Domain logic
 └── API / repository
          ↓
     Backend services
```

### Internal Workflow
An update enters through a UI event or external synchronization source, passes through the selected state/cache boundary, updates immutable or reactive state, notifies relevant subscribers, and causes React to render the affected consumers.

### Data Flow
```text
Intent
  ↓
Action / Mutation
  ↓
Middleware / Network
  ↓
Reducer OR Query Cache
  ↓
Subscription / Selector
  ↓
React Render
```

### Performance Characteristics
- Prefer narrow subscriptions and selectors.
- Avoid duplicating server state in multiple stores.
- Measure render fan-out and cache growth.
- Batch related updates when the library/runtime supports it.
- Remove stale listeners and unused cache entries.

### Memory Considerations
- Large normalized stores can retain unused entities.
- Query caches require explicit freshness and garbage-collection policies.
- Subscriptions must be cleaned up.
- Persisted state should be intentionally scoped and versioned.

### React Integration
Use typed hooks or query hooks at feature boundaries. Keep presentational components focused on rendering and user interaction; keep domain/state logic in reusable feature modules.

### Production Use Case
A production team can use **Context fundamentals** to make ownership explicit, reduce unnecessary renders, isolate failure boundaries and establish consistent debugging and testing workflows.

### Enterprise Example
In a multi-team application, the shared state contract should be versioned and documented. Domain state, server cache, authentication, UI state and analytics should not become one undifferentiated global store.

### Code Example 1
```tsx
import { createContext, useContext, useMemo } from "react";

type Session = { userId: string } | null;
const SessionContext = createContext<Session>(null);

export function SessionProvider({
  session,
  children,
}: { session: Session; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const value = useMemo(() => session, [session]);
  return (
    <SessionContext.Provider value={value}>
      {children}
    </SessionContext.Provider>
  );
}

export const useSession = () => useContext(SessionContext);
```

### Code Example 2
```tsx
// Prefer immutable updates and keep derived values out of stored state.
const state = { user: { id: "u1", name: "Asha" } };
const next = {
  ...state,
  user: { ...state.user, name: "Maya" },
};

console.log(state.user.name); // Asha
console.log(next.user.name);  // Maya
```

### Advanced Production Example
```tsx
// Feature-based boundary: keep state access behind a small public API.
export type Order = {
  id: string;
  status: "pending" | "paid" | "failed";
};

export function selectOrderStatus(
  orders: Record<string, Order>,
  id: string,
): Order["status"] | "unknown" {
  return orders[id]?.status ?? "unknown";
}
```

### Folder Structure
```text
src/
├── app/
│   ├── store.ts
│   └── providers/
├── features/
│   └── orders/
│       ├── components/
│       ├── hooks/
│       ├── api/
│       ├── selectors/
│       ├── model/
│       └── tests/
├── shared/
│   ├── ui/
│   └── types/
└── infrastructure/
    ├── logging/
    └── analytics/
```

### Expected Output
The state transition is deterministic and only the consumers that depend on the changed state should need to update. Server data should remain synchronized through the selected cache/query abstraction.

### ASCII State Diagram
```text
             ┌───────────────┐
             │   React UI    │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Intent/Event  │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │ Store / Query Cache     │
        └───────────┬─────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Selectors /   │
             │ Query Hooks   │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
                 React UI
```

### Performance Notes
Use React DevTools Profiler to identify expensive renders and library-specific DevTools to inspect state/cache transitions. Optimize subscription granularity before introducing complex memoization.

### Security Considerations
- Never treat UI state as an authorization boundary.
- Do not persist secrets unnecessarily.
- Redact tokens and personal data from logs and DevTools captures.
- Validate server responses before storing them in sensitive workflows.

### Advantages
- Explicit state ownership
- Predictable updates
- Strong debugging options
- Testable architecture
- Scales when boundaries are well designed

### Disadvantages
- Additional abstraction and learning cost
- Poorly designed global state can become tightly coupled
- Cache invalidation and synchronization are complex

### Trade-offs
| Requirement | Prefer | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Local UI | React state | Global store |
| Server data | RTK Query / TanStack Query / Apollo | Manual duplicate cache |
| Cross-cutting low-frequency config | Context | Giant global store |
| Complex client workflows | Redux Toolkit / state machine | Scattered effects |
| Tiny isolated store | Zustand / Jotai | Heavy architecture without need |

### Best Practices
1. Define ownership before selecting a library.
2. Keep server state in a server-state cache.
3. Normalize large relational client state when appropriate.
4. Keep selectors focused.
5. Prefer feature boundaries.
6. Instrument important transitions.
7. Test behavior, not implementation details.

### Anti-patterns
- One global store for everything
- Duplicating query data into Redux without a clear reason
- Persisting sensitive tokens by default
- Storing derived values that can be computed
- Calling network APIs directly from arbitrary UI components

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing client state with server state.
- Overusing Context for high-frequency updates.
- Mutating state outside the library's supported mechanisms.
- Ignoring cache invalidation.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce the state transition.
2. Inspect the action/event or query mutation.
3. Inspect the store/cache before and after.
4. Check selector outputs.
5. Profile affected React components.
6. Inspect network requests and cache headers.
7. Check for duplicated subscriptions or stale closures.

### Common Interview Traps
- 'Redux is only for global state.'
- 'Context replaces Redux in every application.'
- 'React Query is a global state manager.'
- 'More memoization always improves performance.'
- 'Frontend role checks are authorization.'

3. What happens under concurrent updates?
4. How is stale data invalidated?
5. How would you test failure and recovery?
6. What is the memory/caching cost?
7. How would this scale across 20 frontend teams?

### System Design Discussion
Define state domains, ownership boundaries, API contracts, cache policy, persistence policy, cross-tab behavior, observability, testing strategy, migration strategy and rollback plan.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] State has a clear owner
- [ ] Server state is not unnecessarily duplicated
- [ ] Updates are predictable and immutable
- [ ] Selectors/subscriptions are appropriately narrow
- [ ] Loading/error/empty states exist
- [ ] Sensitive data is protected
- [ ] Tests cover success and failure
- [ ] Production telemetry is available

### 2-minute Interview Answer

### 5-minute Deep Explanation

- Avoid duplicating server state in multiple stores.
- Measure render fan-out and cache growth.
- Batch related updates when the library/runtime supports it.
- Remove stale listeners and unused cache entries.

### Memory Considerations
- Large normalized stores can retain unused entities.
- Query caches require explicit freshness and garbage-collection policies.
- Subscriptions must be cleaned up.
- Persisted state should be intentionally scoped and versioned.

### React Integration
Use typed hooks or query hooks at feature boundaries. Keep presentational components focused on rendering and user interaction; keep domain/state logic in reusable feature modules.

### Production Use Case
A production team can use **Context versus Redux** to make ownership explicit, reduce unnecessary renders, isolate failure boundaries and establish consistent debugging and testing workflows.

### Enterprise Example
In a multi-team application, the shared state contract should be versioned and documented. Domain state, server cache, authentication, UI state and analytics should not become one undifferentiated global store.

### Code Example 1
```tsx
import { configureStore, createSlice, PayloadAction } from "@reduxjs/toolkit";

type CounterState = { value: number };

const counterSlice = createSlice({
  name: "counter",
  initialState: { value: 0 } satisfies CounterState,
  reducers: {
    increment(state, action: PayloadAction<number>) {
      state.value += action.payload; // Immer safely produces immutable updates.
    },
  },
});

export const store = configureStore({
  reducer: { counter: counterSlice.reducer },
});

store.dispatch(counterSlice.actions.increment(1));
console.log(store.getState().counter.value); // 1
```

### Code Example 2
```tsx
// Prefer immutable updates and keep derived values out of stored state.
const state = { user: { id: "u1", name: "Asha" } };
const next = {
  ...state,
  user: { ...state.user, name: "Maya" },
};

console.log(state.user.name); // Asha
console.log(next.user.name);  // Maya
```

### Advanced Production Example
```tsx
// Feature-based boundary: keep state access behind a small public API.
export type Order = {
  id: string;
  status: "pending" | "paid" | "failed";
};

export function selectOrderStatus(
  orders: Record<string, Order>,
  id: string,
): Order["status"] | "unknown" {
  return orders[id]?.status ?? "unknown";
}
```

### Folder Structure
```text
src/
├── app/
│   ├── store.ts
│   └── providers/
├── features/
│   └── orders/
│       ├── components/
│       ├── hooks/
│       ├── api/
│       ├── selectors/
│       ├── model/
│       └── tests/
├── shared/
│   ├── ui/
│   └── types/
└── infrastructure/
    ├── logging/
    └── analytics/
```

### Expected Output
The state transition is deterministic and only the consumers that depend on the changed state should need to update. Server data should remain synchronized through the selected cache/query abstraction.

### ASCII State Diagram
```text
             ┌───────────────┐
             │   React UI    │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Intent/Event  │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │ Store / Query Cache     │
        └───────────┬─────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Selectors /   │
             │ Query Hooks   │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
                 React UI
```

### Performance Notes
Use React DevTools Profiler to identify expensive renders and library-specific DevTools to inspect state/cache transitions. Optimize subscription granularity before introducing complex memoization.

### Security Considerations
- Never treat UI state as an authorization boundary.
- Do not persist secrets unnecessarily.
- Redact tokens and personal data from logs and DevTools captures.
- Validate server responses before storing them in sensitive workflows.

### Advantages
- Explicit state ownership
- Predictable updates
- Strong debugging options
- Testable architecture
- Scales when boundaries are well designed

### Disadvantages
- Additional abstraction and learning cost
- Poorly designed global state can become tightly coupled
- Cache invalidation and synchronization are complex

### Trade-offs
| Requirement | Prefer | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Local UI | React state | Global store |
| Server data | RTK Query / TanStack Query / Apollo | Manual duplicate cache |
| Cross-cutting low-frequency config | Context | Giant global store |
| Complex client workflows | Redux Toolkit / state machine | Scattered effects |
| Tiny isolated store | Zustand / Jotai | Heavy architecture without need |

### Best Practices
1. Define ownership before selecting a library.
2. Keep server state in a server-state cache.
3. Normalize large relational client state when appropriate.
4. Keep selectors focused.
5. Prefer feature boundaries.
6. Instrument important transitions.
7. Test behavior, not implementation details.

### Anti-patterns
- One global store for everything
- Duplicating query data into Redux without a clear reason
- Persisting sensitive tokens by default
- Storing derived values that can be computed
- Calling network APIs directly from arbitrary UI components

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing client state with server state.
- Overusing Context for high-frequency updates.
- Mutating state outside the library's supported mechanisms.
- Ignoring cache invalidation.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce the state transition.
2. Inspect the action/event or query mutation.
3. Inspect the store/cache before and after.
4. Check selector outputs.
5. Profile affected React components.
6. Inspect network requests and cache headers.
7. Check for duplicated subscriptions or stale closures.

### Common Interview Traps
- 'Redux is only for global state.'
- 'Context replaces Redux in every application.'
- 'React Query is a global state manager.'
- 'More memoization always improves performance.'
- 'Frontend role checks are authorization.'

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
Your enterprise React application is experiencing inconsistent data and unnecessary renders related to **Context versus Redux**. How would you redesign ownership, synchronization, caching and component subscriptions?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the authoritative source of truth?
2. Is this client state or server state?
3. What happens under concurrent updates?
4. How is stale data invalidated?
5. How would you test failure and recovery?
6. What is the memory/caching cost?
7. How would this scale across 20 frontend teams?

### System Design Discussion
Define state domains, ownership boundaries, API contracts, cache policy, persistence policy, cross-tab behavior, observability, testing strategy, migration strategy and rollback plan.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] State has a clear owner
- [ ] Server state is not unnecessarily duplicated
- [ ] Updates are predictable and immutable
- [ ] Selectors/subscriptions are appropriately narrow
- [ ] Loading/error/empty states exist
- [ ] Sensitive data is protected
- [ ] Tests cover success and failure
- [ ] Production telemetry is available

### 30-second Interview Answer
**Context versus Redux** should be chosen based on state ownership and lifecycle. I would first classify the state, then select the smallest suitable mechanism, define the update/cache policy, and validate performance and failure behavior with profiling and tests.

### 2-minute Interview Answer
Start with what **Context versus Redux** solves, then explain the data flow and subscription model. Compare it with the alternatives, discuss cache and memory behavior, and finish with how you would test, monitor, secure and migrate it in production.

### 5-minute Deep Explanation
At Staff/Principal level, discuss **Context versus Redux** as architecture rather than API syntax: ownership, consistency, synchronization, cache invalidation, update fan-out, memory retention, failure recovery, observability, team boundaries, deployment/migration risk and long-term maintainability.

### Assignments

Build an enterprise dashboard with authentication, server data, filters, optimistic updates, caching, error recovery and a feature flag. Keep UI, server and persistent state explicitly separated.

**Answer: B**

- Measure before optimizing.

## Question 124 — Context performance

**Module:** Module 7 – Context API vs Redux  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 5–8 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
Explain **Context performance**, including why it exists, where it belongs in a React application, its runtime/data-flow implications, and the trade-offs an enterprise team should consider.

### Definition
Performance depends on subscription granularity, selector stability, render frequency, cache size and update fan-out. Measure with React DevTools and the library's own tooling before optimizing.

### Overview
State management is primarily an ownership and synchronization problem. A good design identifies the authoritative source, the consumers, the update path, the failure model and the lifecycle of the data.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents duplicated or conflicting state.
- Makes rendering behavior predictable.
- Enables testable business logic and observable production behavior.
- Supports scaling from a single feature to large multi-team applications.

### Architecture
```text
Feature
 ├── UI components
 ├── State / cache boundary
 ├── Selectors / query hooks
 ├── Domain logic
 └── API / repository
          ↓
     Backend services
```

### Internal Workflow
An update enters through a UI event or external synchronization source, passes through the selected state/cache boundary, updates immutable or reactive state, notifies relevant subscribers, and causes React to render the affected consumers.

### Data Flow
```text
Intent
  ↓
Action / Mutation
  ↓
Middleware / Network
  ↓
Reducer OR Query Cache
  ↓
Subscription / Selector
  ↓
React Render
```

- Avoid duplicating server state in multiple stores.
- Measure render fan-out and cache growth.
- Batch related updates when the library/runtime supports it.
- Remove stale listeners and unused cache entries.

### Memory Considerations

- Query caches require explicit freshness and garbage-collection policies.
- Subscriptions must be cleaned up.
- Persisted state should be intentionally scoped and versioned.

### React Integration

### Code Example 1
```tsx
import { createContext, useContext, useMemo } from "react";

type Session = { userId: string } | null;
const SessionContext = createContext<Session>(null);

export function SessionProvider({
  session,
  children,
}: { session: Session; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const value = useMemo(() => session, [session]);
  return (
    <SessionContext.Provider value={value}>
      {children}
    </SessionContext.Provider>
  );
}

export const useSession = () => useContext(SessionContext);
```

### Code Example 2
```tsx
import { useSelector } from "react-redux";

const selectUserName = (state: RootState, id: string) =>
  state.users.entities[id]?.name ?? "Unknown";

export function UserName({ id }: { id: string }) {
  const name = useSelector((state: RootState) => selectUserName(state, id));
  return <span>{name}</span>;
}
```

## Question 126 — Context splitting

**Module:** Module 7 – Context API vs Redux  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 5–8 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
Explain **Context splitting**, including why it exists, where it belongs in a React application, its runtime/data-flow implications, and the trade-offs an enterprise team should consider.

### Definition
Context is excellent for low-frequency cross-cutting values. Frequent, broad updates can cause many consumers to render, so split providers or use an external store when measured fan-out becomes costly.

### Overview
State management is primarily an ownership and synchronization problem. A good design identifies the authoritative source, the consumers, the update path, the failure model and the lifecycle of the data.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents duplicated or conflicting state.
- Makes rendering behavior predictable.
- Enables testable business logic and observable production behavior.
- Supports scaling from a single feature to large multi-team applications.

### Architecture
```text
Feature
 ├── UI components
 ├── State / cache boundary
 ├── Selectors / query hooks
 ├── Domain logic
 └── API / repository
          ↓
     Backend services
```

### Internal Workflow
An update enters through a UI event or external synchronization source, passes through the selected state/cache boundary, updates immutable or reactive state, notifies relevant subscribers, and causes React to render the affected consumers.

### Data Flow
```text
Intent
  ↓
Action / Mutation
  ↓
Middleware / Network
  ↓
Reducer OR Query Cache
  ↓
Subscription / Selector
  ↓
React Render
```

### Performance Characteristics
- Prefer narrow subscriptions and selectors.
- Avoid duplicating server state in multiple stores.
- Measure render fan-out and cache growth.
- Batch related updates when the library/runtime supports it.
- Remove stale listeners and unused cache entries.

### Memory Considerations
- Large normalized stores can retain unused entities.
- Query caches require explicit freshness and garbage-collection policies.
- Subscriptions must be cleaned up.
- Persisted state should be intentionally scoped and versioned.

### React Integration
Use typed hooks or query hooks at feature boundaries. Keep presentational components focused on rendering and user interaction; keep domain/state logic in reusable feature modules.

### Production Use Case
A production team can use **Context splitting** to make ownership explicit, reduce unnecessary renders, isolate failure boundaries and establish consistent debugging and testing workflows.

### Enterprise Example
In a multi-team application, the shared state contract should be versioned and documented. Domain state, server cache, authentication, UI state and analytics should not become one undifferentiated global store.

### Code Example 1
```tsx
import { createContext, useContext, useMemo } from "react";

type Session = { userId: string } | null;
const SessionContext = createContext<Session>(null);

export function SessionProvider({
  session,
  children,
}: { session: Session; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const value = useMemo(() => session, [session]);
  return (
    <SessionContext.Provider value={value}>
      {children}
    </SessionContext.Provider>
  );
}

export const useSession = () => useContext(SessionContext);
```

### Code Example 2
```tsx
// Prefer immutable updates and keep derived values out of stored state.
const state = { user: { id: "u1", name: "Asha" } };
const next = {
  ...state,
  user: { ...state.user, name: "Maya" },
};

console.log(state.user.name); // Asha
console.log(next.user.name);  // Maya
```

### Advanced Production Example
```tsx
// Feature-based boundary: keep state access behind a small public API.
export type Order = {
  id: string;
  status: "pending" | "paid" | "failed";
};

export function selectOrderStatus(
  orders: Record<string, Order>,
  id: string,
): Order["status"] | "unknown" {
  return orders[id]?.status ?? "unknown";
}
```

### Folder Structure
```text
src/
├── app/
│   ├── store.ts
│   └── providers/
├── features/
│   └── orders/
│       ├── components/
│       ├── hooks/
│       ├── api/
│       ├── selectors/
│       ├── model/
│       └── tests/
├── shared/
│   ├── ui/
│   └── types/
└── infrastructure/
    ├── logging/
    └── analytics/
```

### Expected Output
The state transition is deterministic and only the consumers that depend on the changed state should need to update. Server data should remain synchronized through the selected cache/query abstraction.

### ASCII State Diagram
```text
             ┌───────────────┐
             │   React UI    │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Intent/Event  │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │ Store / Query Cache     │
        └───────────┬─────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Selectors /   │
             │ Query Hooks   │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
                 React UI
```

### Performance Notes
Use React DevTools Profiler to identify expensive renders and library-specific DevTools to inspect state/cache transitions. Optimize subscription granularity before introducing complex memoization.

### Security Considerations
- Never treat UI state as an authorization boundary.
- Do not persist secrets unnecessarily.
- Redact tokens and personal data from logs and DevTools captures.
- Validate server responses before storing them in sensitive workflows.

### Advantages
- Explicit state ownership
- Predictable updates
- Strong debugging options
- Testable architecture
- Scales when boundaries are well designed

### Disadvantages
- Additional abstraction and learning cost
- Poorly designed global state can become tightly coupled
- Cache invalidation and synchronization are complex

### Trade-offs
| Requirement | Prefer | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Local UI | React state | Global store |
| Server data | RTK Query / TanStack Query / Apollo | Manual duplicate cache |
| Cross-cutting low-frequency config | Context | Giant global store |
| Complex client workflows | Redux Toolkit / state machine | Scattered effects |
| Tiny isolated store | Zustand / Jotai | Heavy architecture without need |

### Best Practices
1. Define ownership before selecting a library.
2. Keep server state in a server-state cache.
3. Normalize large relational client state when appropriate.
4. Keep selectors focused.
5. Prefer feature boundaries.
6. Instrument important transitions.
7. Test behavior, not implementation details.

### Anti-patterns
- One global store for everything
- Duplicating query data into Redux without a clear reason
- Persisting sensitive tokens by default
- Storing derived values that can be computed
- Calling network APIs directly from arbitrary UI components

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing client state with server state.
- Overusing Context for high-frequency updates.
- Mutating state outside the library's supported mechanisms.
- Ignoring cache invalidation.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce the state transition.
2. Inspect the action/event or query mutation.
3. Inspect the store/cache before and after.
4. Check selector outputs.
5. Profile affected React components.
6. Inspect network requests and cache headers.
7. Check for duplicated subscriptions or stale closures.

### Common Interview Traps
- 'Redux is only for global state.'
- 'Context replaces Redux in every application.'
- 'React Query is a global state manager.'
- 'More memoization always improves performance.'
- 'Frontend role checks are authorization.'

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
Your enterprise React application is experiencing inconsistent data and unnecessary renders related to **Context splitting**. How would you redesign ownership, synchronization, caching and component subscriptions?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the authoritative source of truth?
2. Is this client state or server state?
3. What happens under concurrent updates?
4. How is stale data invalidated?
5. How would you test failure and recovery?
6. What is the memory/caching cost?
7. How would this scale across 20 frontend teams?

### System Design Discussion
Define state domains, ownership boundaries, API contracts, cache policy, persistence policy, cross-tab behavior, observability, testing strategy, migration strategy and rollback plan.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] State has a clear owner
- [ ] Server state is not unnecessarily duplicated
- [ ] Updates are predictable and immutable
- [ ] Selectors/subscriptions are appropriately narrow
- [ ] Loading/error/empty states exist
- [ ] Sensitive data is protected
- [ ] Tests cover success and failure
- [ ] Production telemetry is available

### 30-second Interview Answer

### 2-minute Interview Answer

### 5-minute Deep Explanation

### Assignments

### MCQs

**Answer: B**

A. CSS  B. Narrowing derived/read state  C. Authentication  D. Routing  
**Answer: B**
3. Which tool is designed primarily for server-state caching?

```tsx
  status: "pending" | "paid" | "failed";
};

export function selectOrderStatus(
  orders: Record<string, Order>,
  id: string,
): Order["status"] | "unknown" {
  return orders[id]?.status ?? "unknown";
}
```


### Expected Output
The state transition is deterministic and only the consumers that depend on the changed state should need to update. Server data should remain synchronized through the selected cache/query abstraction.

### ASCII State Diagram
```text
             ┌───────────────┐
             │   React UI    │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
             ┌───────────────┐

             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────┐

        └───────────┬─────────────┘
```

```text
             │ Query Hooks   │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
                 React UI
```

### Performance Notes
Use React DevTools Profiler to identify expensive renders and library-specific DevTools to inspect state/cache transitions. Optimize subscription granularity before introducing complex memoization.

### Security Considerations
- Never treat UI state as an authorization boundary.
- Do not persist secrets unnecessarily.
- Redact tokens and personal data from logs and DevTools captures.
- Validate server responses before storing them in sensitive workflows.

### Advantages
- Explicit state ownership
- Predictable updates
- Strong debugging options
- Testable architecture
- Scales when boundaries are well designed

### Disadvantages
- Additional abstraction and learning cost
- Poorly designed global state can become tightly coupled
- Cache invalidation and synchronization are complex

### Trade-offs
| Requirement | Prefer | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Local UI | React state | Global store |
| Server data | RTK Query / TanStack Query / Apollo | Manual duplicate cache |
| Cross-cutting low-frequency config | Context | Giant global store |
| Complex client workflows | Redux Toolkit / state machine | Scattered effects |
| Tiny isolated store | Zustand / Jotai | Heavy architecture without need |

### Best Practices
1. Define ownership before selecting a library.
2. Keep server state in a server-state cache.
3. Normalize large relational client state when appropriate.
4. Keep selectors focused.
5. Prefer feature boundaries.
6. Instrument important transitions.
7. Test behavior, not implementation details.

### Anti-patterns
- One global store for everything
- Duplicating query data into Redux without a clear reason
- Persisting sensitive tokens by default
- Storing derived values that can be computed
- Calling network APIs directly from arbitrary UI components

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing client state with server state.
- Overusing Context for high-frequency updates.
- Mutating state outside the library's supported mechanisms.
- Ignoring cache invalidation.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce the state transition.
2. Inspect the action/event or query mutation.
3. Inspect the store/cache before and after.
4. Check selector outputs.
5. Profile affected React components.
6. Inspect network requests and cache headers.
7. Check for duplicated subscriptions or stale closures.

### Common Interview Traps
- 'Redux is only for global state.'
- 'Context replaces Redux in every application.'
- 'React Query is a global state manager.'
- 'More memoization always improves performance.'
- 'Frontend role checks are authorization.'

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
Your enterprise React application is experiencing inconsistent data and unnecessary renders related to **Context with memo**. How would you redesign ownership, synchronization, caching and component subscriptions?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the authoritative source of truth?
2. Is this client state or server state?
3. What happens under concurrent updates?
4. How is stale data invalidated?
5. How would you test failure and recovery?
6. What is the memory/caching cost?
7. How would this scale across 20 frontend teams?

### System Design Discussion
Define state domains, ownership boundaries, API contracts, cache policy, persistence policy, cross-tab behavior, observability, testing strategy, migration strategy and rollback plan.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] State has a clear owner
- [ ] Server state is not unnecessarily duplicated
- [ ] Updates are predictable and immutable
- [ ] Selectors/subscriptions are appropriately narrow
- [ ] Loading/error/empty states exist
- [ ] Sensitive data is protected
- [ ] Tests cover success and failure
- [ ] Production telemetry is available

### 30-second Interview Answer
**Context with memo** should be chosen based on state ownership and lifecycle. I would first classify the state, then select the smallest suitable mechanism, define the update/cache policy, and validate performance and failure behavior with profiling and tests.

### 2-minute Interview Answer

### 5-minute Deep Explanation

## Question 129 — Context for configuration

**Module:** Module 7 – Context API vs Redux  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 5–8 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
Explain **Context for configuration**, including why it exists, where it belongs in a React application, its runtime/data-flow implications, and the trade-offs an enterprise team should consider.

### Definition
Context is excellent for low-frequency cross-cutting values. Frequent, broad updates can cause many consumers to render, so split providers or use an external store when measured fan-out becomes costly.

### Overview
State management is primarily an ownership and synchronization problem. A good design identifies the authoritative source, the consumers, the update path, the failure model and the lifecycle of the data.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents duplicated or conflicting state.
- Makes rendering behavior predictable.
- Enables testable business logic and observable production behavior.
- Supports scaling from a single feature to large multi-team applications.

### Architecture
```text
Feature
 ├── UI components
 ├── State / cache boundary
 ├── Selectors / query hooks
 ├── Domain logic
 └── API / repository
          ↓
     Backend services
```

### Internal Workflow
An update enters through a UI event or external synchronization source, passes through the selected state/cache boundary, updates immutable or reactive state, notifies relevant subscribers, and causes React to render the affected consumers.

### Data Flow
```text
Intent
  ↓
Action / Mutation
  ↓
Middleware / Network
  ↓
Reducer OR Query Cache
  ↓
Subscription / Selector
  ↓
React Render
```

### Performance Characteristics
- Prefer narrow subscriptions and selectors.
- Avoid duplicating server state in multiple stores.
- Measure render fan-out and cache growth.
- Batch related updates when the library/runtime supports it.
- Remove stale listeners and unused cache entries.

### Memory Considerations
- Large normalized stores can retain unused entities.
- Query caches require explicit freshness and garbage-collection policies.
- Subscriptions must be cleaned up.
- Persisted state should be intentionally scoped and versioned.

### React Integration
Use typed hooks or query hooks at feature boundaries. Keep presentational components focused on rendering and user interaction; keep domain/state logic in reusable feature modules.

### Production Use Case
A production team can use **Context for configuration** to make ownership explicit, reduce unnecessary renders, isolate failure boundaries and establish consistent debugging and testing workflows.

### Enterprise Example
In a multi-team application, the shared state contract should be versioned and documented. Domain state, server cache, authentication, UI state and analytics should not become one undifferentiated global store.

### Code Example 1
```tsx
import { createContext, useContext, useMemo } from "react";

type Session = { userId: string } | null;
const SessionContext = createContext<Session>(null);

export function SessionProvider({
  session,
  children,
}: { session: Session; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const value = useMemo(() => session, [session]);
  return (
    <SessionContext.Provider value={value}>
      {children}
    </SessionContext.Provider>
  );
}

export const useSession = () => useContext(SessionContext);
```

### Code Example 2
```tsx
// Prefer immutable updates and keep derived values out of stored state.
const state = { user: { id: "u1", name: "Asha" } };
const next = {
  ...state,
  user: { ...state.user, name: "Maya" },
};

console.log(state.user.name); // Asha
console.log(next.user.name);  // Maya
```

### Advanced Production Example

```tsx
  id: string;
  status: "pending" | "paid" | "failed";
};

export function selectOrderStatus(
  orders: Record<string, Order>,
  id: string,
): Order["status"] | "unknown" {
  return orders[id]?.status ?? "unknown";
}
```


## Question 131 — Redux for shared state

**Module:** Module 7 – Context API vs Redux  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 5–8 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
Explain **Redux for shared state**, including why it exists, where it belongs in a React application, its runtime/data-flow implications, and the trade-offs an enterprise team should consider.

### Definition
The concept should be evaluated by ownership, update frequency, consistency requirements, persistence, server synchronization, performance, testing and operational complexity.

### Overview
State management is primarily an ownership and synchronization problem. A good design identifies the authoritative source, the consumers, the update path, the failure model and the lifecycle of the data.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents duplicated or conflicting state.
- Makes rendering behavior predictable.
- Enables testable business logic and observable production behavior.
- Supports scaling from a single feature to large multi-team applications.

### Architecture
```text
Feature
 ├── UI components
 ├── State / cache boundary
 ├── Selectors / query hooks
 ├── Domain logic
 └── API / repository
          ↓
     Backend services
```

### Internal Workflow
An update enters through a UI event or external synchronization source, passes through the selected state/cache boundary, updates immutable or reactive state, notifies relevant subscribers, and causes React to render the affected consumers.

### Data Flow
```text
Intent
  ↓
Action / Mutation
  ↓
Middleware / Network
  ↓
Reducer OR Query Cache
  ↓
Subscription / Selector
  ↓
React Render
```

### Performance Characteristics
- Prefer narrow subscriptions and selectors.
- Avoid duplicating server state in multiple stores.
- Measure render fan-out and cache growth.
- Batch related updates when the library/runtime supports it.
- Remove stale listeners and unused cache entries.

### Memory Considerations
- Large normalized stores can retain unused entities.
- Query caches require explicit freshness and garbage-collection policies.
- Subscriptions must be cleaned up.
- Persisted state should be intentionally scoped and versioned.

### React Integration
Use typed hooks or query hooks at feature boundaries. Keep presentational components focused on rendering and user interaction; keep domain/state logic in reusable feature modules.

### Production Use Case
A production team can use **Redux for shared state** to make ownership explicit, reduce unnecessary renders, isolate failure boundaries and establish consistent debugging and testing workflows.

### Enterprise Example
In a multi-team application, the shared state contract should be versioned and documented. Domain state, server cache, authentication, UI state and analytics should not become one undifferentiated global store.

### Code Example 1
```tsx
import { configureStore, createSlice, PayloadAction } from "@reduxjs/toolkit";

type CounterState = { value: number };

const counterSlice = createSlice({
  name: "counter",
  initialState: { value: 0 } satisfies CounterState,
  reducers: {
    increment(state, action: PayloadAction<number>) {
      state.value += action.payload; // Immer safely produces immutable updates.
    },
  },
});

export const store = configureStore({
  reducer: { counter: counterSlice.reducer },
});

store.dispatch(counterSlice.actions.increment(1));
console.log(store.getState().counter.value); // 1
```

### Code Example 2
```tsx
// Prefer immutable updates and keep derived values out of stored state.
const state = { user: { id: "u1", name: "Asha" } };
const next = {
  ...state,
  user: { ...state.user, name: "Maya" },
};

console.log(state.user.name); // Asha
console.log(next.user.name);  // Maya
```

### Advanced Production Example
```tsx
// Feature-based boundary: keep state access behind a small public API.
export type Order = {
  id: string;
  status: "pending" | "paid" | "failed";
};

export function selectOrderStatus(
  orders: Record<string, Order>,
  id: string,
): Order["status"] | "unknown" {
  return orders[id]?.status ?? "unknown";
}
```

### Folder Structure
```text
src/
├── app/
│   ├── store.ts
│   └── providers/
├── features/
│   └── orders/
│       ├── components/
│       ├── hooks/
│       ├── api/
│       ├── selectors/
│       ├── model/
│       └── tests/
├── shared/
│   ├── ui/
│   └── types/
└── infrastructure/
    ├── logging/
    └── analytics/
```

### Expected Output
The state transition is deterministic and only the consumers that depend on the changed state should need to update. Server data should remain synchronized through the selected cache/query abstraction.

### ASCII State Diagram
```text
             ┌───────────────┐
             │   React UI    │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Intent/Event  │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │ Store / Query Cache     │
        └───────────┬─────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Selectors /   │
             │ Query Hooks   │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
                 React UI
```

### Performance Notes
Use React DevTools Profiler to identify expensive renders and library-specific DevTools to inspect state/cache transitions. Optimize subscription granularity before introducing complex memoization.

### Security Considerations
- Never treat UI state as an authorization boundary.
- Do not persist secrets unnecessarily.
- Redact tokens and personal data from logs and DevTools captures.
- Validate server responses before storing them in sensitive workflows.

### Advantages
- Explicit state ownership
- Predictable updates
- Strong debugging options
- Testable architecture
- Scales when boundaries are well designed

### Disadvantages
- Additional abstraction and learning cost
- Poorly designed global state can become tightly coupled
- Cache invalidation and synchronization are complex

### Trade-offs
| Requirement | Prefer | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Local UI | React state | Global store |
| Server data | RTK Query / TanStack Query / Apollo | Manual duplicate cache |
| Cross-cutting low-frequency config | Context | Giant global store |
| Complex client workflows | Redux Toolkit / state machine | Scattered effects |
| Tiny isolated store | Zustand / Jotai | Heavy architecture without need |

### Best Practices
1. Define ownership before selecting a library.
2. Keep server state in a server-state cache.
3. Normalize large relational client state when appropriate.
4. Keep selectors focused.
5. Prefer feature boundaries.
6. Instrument important transitions.
7. Test behavior, not implementation details.

### Anti-patterns
- One global store for everything
- Duplicating query data into Redux without a clear reason
- Persisting sensitive tokens by default
- Storing derived values that can be computed
- Calling network APIs directly from arbitrary UI components

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing client state with server state.
- Overusing Context for high-frequency updates.
- Mutating state outside the library's supported mechanisms.
- Ignoring cache invalidation.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce the state transition.
2. Inspect the action/event or query mutation.
3. Inspect the store/cache before and after.
4. Check selector outputs.
5. Profile affected React components.
6. Inspect network requests and cache headers.
7. Check for duplicated subscriptions or stale closures.

### Common Interview Traps
- 'Redux is only for global state.'
- 'Context replaces Redux in every application.'
- 'React Query is a global state manager.'
- 'More memoization always improves performance.'
- 'Frontend role checks are authorization.'

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
Your enterprise React application is experiencing inconsistent data and unnecessary renders related to **Redux for shared state**. How would you redesign ownership, synchronization, caching and component subscriptions?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the authoritative source of truth?
2. Is this client state or server state?
3. What happens under concurrent updates?
4. How is stale data invalidated?
5. How would you test failure and recovery?
6. What is the memory/caching cost?
7. How would this scale across 20 frontend teams?

### System Design Discussion
Define state domains, ownership boundaries, API contracts, cache policy, persistence policy, cross-tab behavior, observability, testing strategy, migration strategy and rollback plan.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] State has a clear owner
- [ ] Server state is not unnecessarily duplicated
- [ ] Updates are predictable and immutable
- [ ] Selectors/subscriptions are appropriately narrow
- [ ] Loading/error/empty states exist
- [ ] Sensitive data is protected
- [ ] Tests cover success and failure
- [ ] Production telemetry is available

### 30-second Interview Answer
**Redux for shared state** should be chosen based on state ownership and lifecycle. I would first classify the state, then select the smallest suitable mechanism, define the update/cache policy, and validate performance and failure behavior with profiling and tests.

### 2-minute Interview Answer
Start with what **Redux for shared state** solves, then explain the data flow and subscription model. Compare it with the alternatives, discuss cache and memory behavior, and finish with how you would test, monitor, secure and migrate it in production.

### 5-minute Deep Explanation
At Staff/Principal level, discuss **Redux for shared state** as architecture rather than API syntax: ownership, consistency, synchronization, cache invalidation, update fan-out, memory retention, failure recovery, observability, team boundaries, deployment/migration risk and long-term maintainability.

### Assignments
Design a feature architecture demonstrating **Redux for shared state**. Document state ownership, cache policy, error states, performance budget, testing strategy and migration/rollback strategy.

### Mini Project
Build an enterprise dashboard with authentication, server data, filters, optimistic updates, caching, error recovery and a feature flag. Keep UI, server and persistent state explicitly separated.

### MCQs

A. Modal open  B. API user profile  C. Selected tab  D. Input draft  
**Answer: B**
2. What is a selector primarily useful for?  
A. CSS  B. Narrowing derived/read state  C. Authentication  D. Routing  
**Answer: B**
3. Which tool is designed primarily for server-state caching?  
A. TanStack Query  B. CSS Modules  C. React Router  D. ESLint  
**Answer: A**
4. What is a key Redux Toolkit benefit?  
A. Removes JavaScript  B. Simplifies predictable Redux architecture  C. Replaces HTTP  D. Eliminates React rendering  
**Answer: B**
5. What should be the security boundary for authorization?  
A. UI store  B. CSS  C. Backend/server  D. Selector  
**Answer: C**

Create an intentionally inefficient state flow, profile it, identify the update fan-out, then reduce unnecessary subscriptions and verify the improvement.

### Revision Notes
- Redux for shared state: definition → ownership → data flow → rendering → performance → security → testing → architecture.
- Always distinguish source of truth from derived state.
- Measure before optimizing.

**Redux for shared state → Who owns it? → Who updates it? → Who reads it? → How is it cached? → How is it persisted? → How does it fail?**

```tsx
const SessionContext = createContext<Session>(null);

  session,
  children,
}: { session: Session; children: React.ReactNode }) {
  const value = useMemo(() => session, [session]);
  return (
    <SessionContext.Provider value={value}>
      {children}
    </SessionContext.Provider>
  );
}

export const useSession = () => useContext(SessionContext);
```

```text
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Intent/Event  │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │ Store / Query Cache     │
        └───────────┬─────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Selectors /   │
             │ Query Hooks   │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
                 React UI
```

### Performance Notes
Use React DevTools Profiler to identify expensive renders and library-specific DevTools to inspect state/cache transitions. Optimize subscription granularity before introducing complex memoization.

### Security Considerations
- Never treat UI state as an authorization boundary.
- Do not persist secrets unnecessarily.
- Redact tokens and personal data from logs and DevTools captures.
- Validate server responses before storing them in sensitive workflows.

### Advantages
- Explicit state ownership
- Predictable updates
- Strong debugging options
- Testable architecture
- Scales when boundaries are well designed

### Disadvantages
- Additional abstraction and learning cost
- Poorly designed global state can become tightly coupled
- Cache invalidation and synchronization are complex

### Trade-offs
| Requirement | Prefer | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| Local UI | React state | Global store |
| Server data | RTK Query / TanStack Query / Apollo | Manual duplicate cache |
| Cross-cutting low-frequency config | Context | Giant global store |
| Complex client workflows | Redux Toolkit / state machine | Scattered effects |
| Tiny isolated store | Zustand / Jotai | Heavy architecture without need |

### Best Practices
1. Define ownership before selecting a library.
2. Keep server state in a server-state cache.
3. Normalize large relational client state when appropriate.
4. Keep selectors focused.
5. Prefer feature boundaries.
6. Instrument important transitions.
7. Test behavior, not implementation details.

### Anti-patterns
- One global store for everything
- Duplicating query data into Redux without a clear reason
- Persisting sensitive tokens by default
- Storing derived values that can be computed
- Calling network APIs directly from arbitrary UI components

### Common Mistakes
- Confusing client state with server state.
- Overusing Context for high-frequency updates.
- Mutating state outside the library's supported mechanisms.
- Ignoring cache invalidation.

### Debugging Tips
1. Reproduce the state transition.
2. Inspect the action/event or query mutation.
3. Inspect the store/cache before and after.
4. Check selector outputs.
5. Profile affected React components.
6. Inspect network requests and cache headers.
7. Check for duplicated subscriptions or stale closures.

### Common Interview Traps
- 'Redux is only for global state.'
- 'Context replaces Redux in every application.'
- 'React Query is a global state manager.'
- 'More memoization always improves performance.'
- 'Frontend role checks are authorization.'

### Scenario-Based Interview Question
Your enterprise React application is experiencing inconsistent data and unnecessary renders related to **When Redux is better**. How would you redesign ownership, synchronization, caching and component subscriptions?

### Senior Follow-up Questions
1. What is the authoritative source of truth?
2. Is this client state or server state?
3. What happens under concurrent updates?
4. How is stale data invalidated?
5. How would you test failure and recovery?
6. What is the memory/caching cost?
7. How would this scale across 20 frontend teams?

### System Design Discussion
Define state domains, ownership boundaries, API contracts, cache policy, persistence policy, cross-tab behavior, observability, testing strategy, migration strategy and rollback plan.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] State has a clear owner
- [ ] Server state is not unnecessarily duplicated
- [ ] Updates are predictable and immutable
- [ ] Selectors/subscriptions are appropriately narrow
- [ ] Loading/error/empty states exist
- [ ] Sensitive data is protected
- [ ] Tests cover success and failure
- [ ] Production telemetry is available

### 30-second Interview Answer
**When Redux is better** should be chosen based on state ownership and lifecycle. I would first classify the state, then select the smallest suitable mechanism, define the update/cache policy, and validate performance and failure behavior with profiling and tests.

### 2-minute Interview Answer
Start with what **When Redux is better** solves, then explain the data flow and subscription model. Compare it with the alternatives, discuss cache and memory behavior, and finish with how you would test, monitor, secure and migrate it in production.

### 5-minute Deep Explanation
At Staff/Principal level, discuss **When Redux is better** as architecture rather than API syntax: ownership, consistency, synchronization, cache invalidation, update fan-out, memory retention, failure recovery, observability, team boundaries, deployment/migration risk and long-term maintainability.

### Assignments
Design a feature architecture demonstrating **When Redux is better**. Document state ownership, cache policy, error states, performance budget, testing strategy and migration/rollback strategy.

### Mini Project
Build an enterprise dashboard with authentication, server data, filters, optimistic updates, caching, error recovery and a feature flag. Keep UI, server and persistent state explicitly separated.

### MCQs
1. Which is usually server state?  
A. Modal open  B. API user profile  C. Selected tab  D. Input draft  
**Answer: B**
2. What is a selector primarily useful for?  
A. CSS  B. Narrowing derived/read state  C. Authentication  D. Routing  
**Answer: B**
3. Which tool is designed primarily for server-state caching?  
A. TanStack Query  B. CSS Modules  C. React Router  D. ESLint  
**Answer: A**
4. What is a key Redux Toolkit benefit?  
A. Removes JavaScript  B. Simplifies predictable Redux architecture  C. Replaces HTTP  D. Eliminates React rendering  
**Answer: B**
5. What should be the security boundary for authorization?  
A. UI store  B. CSS  C. Backend/server  D. Selector  
**Answer: C**

### Coding Exercise
Implement **When Redux is better** using TypeScript and React 19+. Include loading, error and empty states, a test, and a performance note.

### Debugging Exercise
Create an intentionally inefficient state flow, profile it, identify the update fan-out, then reduce unnecessary subscriptions and verify the improvement.

### Revision Notes
- When Redux is better: definition → ownership → data flow → rendering → performance → security → testing → architecture.
- Always distinguish source of truth from derived state.
- Measure before optimizing.

### Cheat Sheet
**When Redux is better → Who owns it? → Who updates it? → Who reads it? → How is it cached? → How is it persisted? → How does it fail?**

## Question 134 — Migration from Context to Redux

**Module:** Module 7 – Context API vs Redux  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐ Medium  
**Experience Level:** 5–8 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Question
Explain **Migration from Context to Redux**, including why it exists, where it belongs in a React application, its runtime/data-flow implications, and the trade-offs an enterprise team should consider.

### Definition
Context is excellent for low-frequency cross-cutting values. Frequent, broad updates can cause many consumers to render, so split providers or use an external store when measured fan-out becomes costly.

### Overview
State management is primarily an ownership and synchronization problem. A good design identifies the authoritative source, the consumers, the update path, the failure model and the lifecycle of the data.

### Why It Matters
- Prevents duplicated or conflicting state.
- Makes rendering behavior predictable.
- Enables testable business logic and observable production behavior.
- Supports scaling from a single feature to large multi-team applications.

### Architecture
```text
Feature
 ├── UI components
 ├── State / cache boundary
 ├── Selectors / query hooks
 ├── Domain logic
 └── API / repository
          ↓
     Backend services
```

### Internal Workflow
An update enters through a UI event or external synchronization source, passes through the selected state/cache boundary, updates immutable or reactive state, notifies relevant subscribers, and causes React to render the affected consumers.

### Data Flow
```text
Intent
  ↓
Action / Mutation
  ↓
Middleware / Network
  ↓
Reducer OR Query Cache
  ↓
Subscription / Selector
  ↓
React Render
```

### Performance Characteristics
- Prefer narrow subscriptions and selectors.
- Avoid duplicating server state in multiple stores.
- Measure render fan-out and cache growth.
- Batch related updates when the library/runtime supports it.
- Remove stale listeners and unused cache entries.

### Memory Considerations
- Large normalized stores can retain unused entities.
- Query caches require explicit freshness and garbage-collection policies.
- Subscriptions must be cleaned up.
- Persisted state should be intentionally scoped and versioned.

### React Integration
Use typed hooks or query hooks at feature boundaries. Keep presentational components focused on rendering and user interaction; keep domain/state logic in reusable feature modules.

### Production Use Case
A production team can use **Migration from Context to Redux** to make ownership explicit, reduce unnecessary renders, isolate failure boundaries and establish consistent debugging and testing workflows.

### Enterprise Example
In a multi-team application, the shared state contract should be versioned and documented. Domain state, server cache, authentication, UI state and analytics should not become one undifferentiated global store.

### Code Example 1
```tsx
import { configureStore, createSlice, PayloadAction } from "@reduxjs/toolkit";

type CounterState = { value: number };

const counterSlice = createSlice({
  name: "counter",
  initialState: { value: 0 } satisfies CounterState,
  reducers: {
    increment(state, action: PayloadAction<number>) {
      state.value += action.payload; // Immer safely produces immutable updates.
    },
  },
});

export const store = configureStore({
  reducer: { counter: counterSlice.reducer },
});

store.dispatch(counterSlice.actions.increment(1));
console.log(store.getState().counter.value); // 1
```

### Code Example 2
```tsx
// Prefer immutable updates and keep derived values out of stored state.
const state = { user: { id: "u1", name: "Asha" } };
const next = {
  ...state,
  user: { ...state.user, name: "Maya" },
};

console.log(state.user.name); // Asha
console.log(next.user.name);  // Maya
```

### Advanced Production Example
```tsx
// Feature-based boundary: keep state access behind a small public API.
export type Order = {
  id: string;
  status: "pending" | "paid" | "failed";
};

export function selectOrderStatus(
  orders: Record<string, Order>,
  id: string,
): Order["status"] | "unknown" {
  return orders[id]?.status ?? "unknown";
}
```

### Folder Structure
```text
src/
├── app/
│   ├── store.ts
│   └── providers/
├── features/
│   └── orders/
│       ├── components/
│       ├── hooks/
│       ├── api/
│       ├── selectors/
│       ├── model/
│       └── tests/
├── shared/
│   ├── ui/
│   └── types/
└── infrastructure/
    ├── logging/
    └── analytics/
```

### Expected Output
The state transition is deterministic and only the consumers that depend on the changed state should need to update. Server data should remain synchronized through the selected cache/query abstraction.

```text
             │ Intent/Event  │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
        ┌─────────────────────────┐
        │ Store / Query Cache     │
        └───────────┬─────────────┘
                    │
                    ▼
             ┌───────────────┐
             │ Selectors /   │
             │ Query Hooks   │
             └───────┬───────┘
                     │
                     ▼
                 React UI
```

- Validate server responses before storing them in sensitive workflows.
